sections.title: How far apart are the two points?
sections.label: Length
sections.intro: Draw the right triangle under the segment. The horizontal and vertical displacements give its two shorter sides.

blocks.html: Distance is \(\sqrt{(x_2-x_1)^2+(y_2-y_1)^2}\). A negative displacement still contributes a positive square.

figure.alt: A line segment, its midpoint and a rise–run triangle
figure.caption: The same direction is used for the horizontal and vertical differences.

blocks.prompt:
The ends of a straight survey baseline are \(P(-11,1)\) and \(Q(-7,23)\).

Find the exact length of the baseline.
blocks.hint: Use the squares of coordinate differences.
blocks.solution:
The changes from \(P\) to \(Q\) are \(4\) horizontally and \(22\) vertically.

Pythagoras gives \(PQ^2=500\).

\(10\sqrt{5}\)

sections.title: How can I recover a missing endpoint?
sections.label: Midpoint
sections.intro: Write a separate average for x and for y. Read each equation backwards to recover the unknown coordinate.

blocks.html: For a segment with midpoint \(M\), its missing end is found by doubling each coordinate of \(M\) and subtracting the corresponding known coordinate.

blocks.prompt:
A segment has endpoint \(P(3,3)\) and midpoint \(M(5,-10)\).

Find the other endpoint.
blocks.hint: Use each midpoint equation in reverse.
blocks.solution:
Double the midpoint coordinate and subtract the known endpoint: \(Q=(5,-10)\times2-(3,3)\).

\((7,-23)\)

blocks.html: Averaging x with y mixes the directions.

\((9,-23)\)

blocks.html: Substitute the recovered end into the original coordinate averages.

sections.title: How do I give a signed gradient?
sections.label: Gradient
sections.intro: Keep the same point order in both differences. A graph slopes upwards to the right when the gradient is positive.

blocks.html: Gradient is \(\frac{\Delta y}{\Delta x}\). It is undefined when the horizontal change is zero.

blocks.prompt:
The ends of a straight survey baseline are \(P(-2,6)\) and \(Q(2,38)\).

Find the gradient of the baseline.
blocks.hint: Subtract in the same point order in both differences.
blocks.solution:
Use vertical change over horizontal change: \(\frac{32}{4}\).

\(8\)

blocks.html: A negative gradient can come from a positive horizontal change and a negative vertical change.

sections.title: What do parallel lines have in common?
sections.label: Parallel
sections.intro: Horizontal progress of one unit produces the same vertical change on parallel lines.

blocks.html: Parallel non-vertical lines have equal gradients. Distinct intercepts give distinct parallel lines.

blocks.prompt:
The line \(L\) has equation \(3x+11y=1\). A line \(K\) passes through \(P(11,13)\) and is parallel to \(L\).

Find the gradient of \(K\).
blocks.hint: Divide the x-coefficient of the rearranged equation by the coefficient of y.
blocks.solution:
Rearrange the given equation to obtain \(y=-\frac{3}{11}x+\frac{1}{11}\). Parallel lines have equal gradients.

\(-\frac{3}{11}\)

blocks.html: A common gradient and intercept describe the same line.

blocks.prompt:

blocks.hint: Divide the x-coefficient of the rearranged equation by the coefficient of y.
blocks.solution:
Rearrange the given equation to obtain \(y=-\frac{3}{11}x+\frac{3}{11}\). Parallel lines have equal gradients.

\(-\frac{3}{11}\)

blocks.html: Rearrange the given equation for y before reading the gradient.

sections.title: Which gradient gives a right angle?
sections.label: Perpendicular
sections.intro: Switch rise and run, then change one sign. This makes the gradient the negative reciprocal.

blocks.html: Non-vertical perpendicular lines have gradient product \(-1\). A horizontal line and a vertical line are perpendicular.

figure.alt: A segment AB and its perpendicular bisector meeting at M
figure.caption: The lines meet at a right angle at the midpoint M.

blocks.prompt:
A segment joins \(A(0,-12)\) to \(B(4,18)\). The line \(K\) is perpendicular to \(AB\) and passes through \(P(22,-8)\).

Find an equation of \(K\).
blocks.hint: Use the negative reciprocal gradient and the appropriate point on the required line.
blocks.solution:
\(AB\) has gradient \(\frac{15}{2}\), so the perpendicular gradient is \(-\frac{2}{15}\).

Substitute \((22,-8)\) into \(y=mx+c\) to find \(c=-\frac{76}{15}\).

\(y=-\frac{2}{15}x-\frac{76}{15}\)

blocks.html: Negating without taking the reciprocal normally produces the wrong angle.

blocks.html: Test a horizontal or vertical line separately before using a reciprocal.

sections.title: Where does a perpendicular bisector pass?
sections.label: Bisector
sections.intro: Its name gives two conditions. The required line is perpendicular and passes through the midpoint.

blocks.html: A point lies on a perpendicular bisector precisely when it is the same distance from the two ends.

blocks.prompt:
A segment joins \(A(-5,-15)\) to \(B(-1,21)\). Its midfield boundary is the perpendicular bisector.

Find an equation of the perpendicular bisector.
blocks.hint: Use the negative reciprocal gradient and the appropriate point on the required line.
blocks.solution:
\(AB\) has gradient \(9\), so the perpendicular gradient is \(-\frac{1}{9}\).

The midpoint is \((-3,3)\). Substitute \((-3,3)\) into \(y=mx+c\) to find \(c=\frac{8}{3}\).

\(y=-\frac{1}{9}x+\frac{8}{3}\)

blocks.html: The perpendicular through an endpoint is a different line.

examples.title: Two parallel route lines
examples.question:
The line \(L\) has equation \(3x+11y=0\). A line \(K\) passes through \(P(11,12)\) and is parallel to \(L\).

  1. Find the gradient of \(K\).

    [2]

  2. Find an equation for \(K\).

    [2]

  3. Find the y-coordinate of \(K\) when \(x=22\).

    [2]
solution: (a) Rearrange the given equation to obtain \(y=-\frac{3}{11}x\). Parallel lines have equal gradients.
(b) Substitute \((11,12)\) into \(y=mx+c\) using \(m=-\frac{3}{11}\). The intercept is \(15\).
(c) Substitute the new horizontal coordinate into \(y=-\frac{3}{11}x+15\).

sections.title: Where do two lines meet?
sections.label: Meeting
sections.intro: At the intersection the same ordered pair satisfies both equations.

blocks.html: If both equations give \(y\), set their right-hand sides equal, then substitute the resulting x-coordinate back.

figure.alt: Two straight lines cross at a marked point
figure.caption: The point of intersection satisfies both equations.

blocks.prompt:
A motion sensor gives the position \(y=2x+47\). A second sensor gives \(14x+y=-113\).

Find the point where the lines cross.
blocks.hint: Solve the equations simultaneously and then substitute.
blocks.solution:
The second line is \(y=-14x-113\). Set the two expressions for \(y\) equal.

Rearranging gives \(16x=-160\). Substitute the resulting x-coordinate back to get \(y=27\).

\((-10,27)\)

  1. Find the point where the lines cross.

    [2]

  2. Find the exact distance from \((-13,23)\) to the intersection.

    [2]

  3. Which model has the larger y-value one unit to the right of the intersection? Give the difference.

    [2]
solution: (a) The second line is \(y=-14x-127\). Set the two expressions for \(y\) equal.
Rearranging gives \(16x=-176\). Substitute the resulting x-coordinate back to get \(y=27\).
(b) The coordinate differences are \(2\) and \(4\). Apply Pythagoras.
(c) One unit to the right, the first output changes by \(2\) and the second by \(-14\).

revision.body:
How does a point fix the position of a line?

Either use \(y=mx+c\) and solve for \(c\), or write \(y-y_1=m(x-x_1)\).

Where do two lines meet?

If both equations give \(y\), set their right-hand sides equal, then substitute the resulting x-coordinate back.

When is standard form useful?

Forms such as \(ax+by=c\) and \(y=mx+c\) describe the same line when one is obtained by valid rearrangement.

revision.body:
Which operations make a straight-line pattern?

In \(\sqrt y=a+b/x\), the two axis variables can be \(Y=\sqrt y\) and \(X=1/x\). The relation then has the form \(Y=bX+a\).

How can a power model give a straight line?

For \(y=Ax^n\), plot \(\log y\) against \(\log x\). The gradient is \(n\) and the intercept is \(\log A\).

How does a logarithm undo an exponential model?

If \(y=e^{ax^2+b}\), use \(Y=\ln y\) and \(X=x^2\). In \(Y=aX+b\), identify the constants by their roles.

Which numbers belong in the gradient formula?

Find the gradient in transformed coordinates, substitute one row for the intercept, and test a third row.

What can a constant multiplying factor tell me?

For \(y=Ab^x\), a step of \(h\) gives an output ratio of \(b^h\), so recover \(b\) by taking a positive root.

How do I use the original model to predict?

A transformed intercept may give a parameter such as a logarithm of the initial value. Apply the inverse operation to interpret it.
